sections.title: Space, time and the observable universe
sections.text:
The universe includes space, time, matter and energy. Matter ranges from elementary particles to planets, stars and galaxies. Radiation carries energy through space. Gravity connects the behaviour of these components across enormous distances. Cosmology studies the universe as a whole: its large-scale structure, history and possible future.

The observable universe is the region from which signals have had time to reach us during cosmic history. It is an observational limit, not a physical wall. Light takes time to travel, so observing a distant galaxy also means observing an earlier stage of its development. A telescope is therefore both a collecting instrument and a way of investigating the past. The entire universe may extend beyond what is observable; its full size is not established by observations of the accessible region alone.

Scientific descriptions distinguish observations from models. A spectrum or measured background temperature is an observation. A cosmological model connects many observations through physical laws. A successful model explains existing evidence and produces testable predictions, but it does not turn unanswered questions into established facts.

sections.title: Astronomical distances and measurement
sections.text:
The astronomical unit, AU, is a convenient scale for the Solar System. One AU is exactly 149,597,870,700 metres, approximately the mean Earth–Sun distance. A light-year is the distance light travels in vacuum in one Julian year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres. It measures distance even though its name contains “year”. The parsec is related to stellar parallax: one parsec is the distance at which one AU subtends one arcsecond, and equals about 3.26 light-years.

Parallax is an apparent shift caused by a change in the observer's position. Nearby stars appear to shift slightly against more distant stars as Earth moves around the Sun. For the conventional annual parallax angle,

$$d=\frac{1}{p}.$$

Here $d$ is distance in parsecs and $p$ is parallax in arcseconds. A hypothetical star with $p=0.2$ arcseconds is $1/0.2=5$ parsecs away. This relation uses these particular units; substituting degrees without conversion gives the wrong result. Smaller parallax means greater distance, while extremely small angles demand more precise measurement.

Distance can also be related to travel time through $d=ct$, where $c$ is the vacuum speed of light, approximately $3.00\times10^8$ metres per second, and $t$ is time in seconds. Light from an object ten light-years away takes approximately ten years to arrive in a simple local-distance interpretation. At cosmological scales, expansion makes the relationship between travel time and present distance more complicated.

sections.title: The hot Big Bang model
sections.text:
The Big Bang model describes an early hot, dense universe followed by expansion and cooling. It is not an ordinary explosion throwing matter from a central point into surrounding empty space. On sufficiently large scales, distances between unbound regions increase as the geometry of space evolves. Gravitationally bound systems such as the Solar System do not simply expand at the same rate as the cosmic background.

In the early universe, temperatures were too high for stable neutral atoms. As cooling proceeded, light nuclei formed, especially hydrogen and helium nuclei. Much later, electrons combined with nuclei to form neutral atoms, and radiation could travel much more freely. Small differences in density grew under gravity, eventually producing stars, galaxies and larger structures. This sequence explains why the universe did not begin with already formed planets and mature stars.

The model describes development from an early state; it does not establish what, if anything, preceded that state. Inflation is a proposed early episode of very rapid expansion that addresses several cosmological questions, but particular inflationary mechanisms remain subjects of research. Dark matter and dark energy also represent distinct scientific problems: evidence for their effects does not mean their physical nature is completely understood.

sections.title: Evidence for cosmic evolution
sections.text:
Three major lines of evidence support the hot Big Bang framework. First, distant galaxies exhibit systematic cosmological redshifts consistent with expansion. Second, the cosmic microwave background is widespread relic radiation with a thermal spectrum. Third, observed abundances of light elements broadly agree with calculations of early-universe nuclear processes. These independent observations constrain the same physical history. [NASA: universe overview](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/).

Redshift describes an increase in wavelength:

$$z=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{observed}}-\lambda_{\mathrm{emitted}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{emitted}}}.$$

Both wavelengths must use the same units, so $z$ is dimensionless. If a spectral feature emitted at 500 nanometres is observed at 550 nanometres, its redshift is $(550-500)/500=0.10$. Cosmological expansion, local motion and gravitational effects can contribute to wavelength shifts; the interpretation depends on context.

At relatively small cosmological distances, an approximate expansion relation is $v\approx H_0d$, where $v$ is recession velocity, $d$ is distance and $H_0$ is the present expansion parameter. It is an approximation rather than a universal high-redshift velocity formula. Different methods of measuring expansion remain an active research area, so an introductory account should not present one precision value as beyond scientific dispute.

sections.title: Matter, gravity and the future
sections.text:
Ordinary matter includes atoms and their constituents. Dark matter is inferred from gravitational effects such as galaxy dynamics and gravitational lensing; it is not merely ordinary matter that happens to look dark. Dark energy is the name associated with the cause of accelerated cosmic expansion in the standard model. These terms describe different roles and should not be used interchangeably.

Cosmic evolution connects the smallest and largest scales. Nuclear reactions created light elements; stars later built many heavier nuclei; gravity assembled galaxies; chemical reactions eventually produced complex compounds. The future depends on the universe's contents and the behaviour of expansion. Predictions are conditional on models, especially where the underlying nature of dark energy remains uncertain.

**Cosmic time and uncertainty.** The standard cosmological interpretation gives an age of about 13.8 billion years for the universe. This is an inference from observations fitted to a physical model, rather than a clock read directly from a distant object. Age is different from the present distance to the most distant observable regions, because space expanded while their light was travelling. Multiplying age by the present speed of light therefore does not by itself give the present radius of the observable universe.

**Redshift and look-back observations.** A galaxy spectrum contains identifiable features whose observed wavelengths can be compared with laboratory wavelengths. Several matching features make identification more secure than a single ambiguous line. Redshift supplies information about cosmic expansion, while distance estimation requires a cosmological model or independent distance indicators. Astronomers also account for dust, instrument response and local motions. Agreement among different measurement techniques is more informative than one isolated image.

**Why cosmic expansion has no ordinary central viewpoint.** In a homogeneous expanding model, observers in different sufficiently distant galaxies can each see other unbound galaxies receding on average. This does not make every observer the physical centre of an explosion. The relationship is among distances throughout the expanding geometry. Familiar surface analogies can help visualize this relationship, but they must not be treated as literal descriptions of an extra surrounding space.

questions.prompt: A scientist reports that a star is located five light-years away. The measurement represents:

options.D: The duration of one Earth day

questions.explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in vacuum over one Julian year.

questions.prompt: The cosmological redshift of light from a sufficiently distant galaxy is primarily interpreted in the standard cosmological model as evidence of:

options.A: Light becoming heavier in intergalactic space
options.B: The expansion of the universe stretching radiation wavelengths
options.C: The Earth expanding more rapidly than the Sun

questions.explanation: Cosmological expansion increases the wavelength of radiation traveling through expanding space. Local motions can also contribute Doppler shifts.

questions.prompt: Which observation is especially important as evidence for an early hot, dense universe?
questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background is relic radiation from the early universe, now observed predominantly at microwave wavelengths.

questions.prompt: If two stars are observed using the same parallax baseline, the more distant star generally has:

options.C: A permanently fixed apparent magnitude of zero

questions.explanation: Parallax decreases as distance increases for a fixed baseline. Astronomical parallax provides a geometric method for determining stellar distances.
